statement: Weekly direct sets per muscle group, calculated from Butters University (indirect sets count about half). Start: beginner 10 (band 8–12), intermediate 12 (band 10–15), advanced 15 (band 10–20). Age 60+: 10, at most 12. Two or fewer sessions a week: 8–10. A cut does not lower volume (at least 10 sets). Go higher only when recovery and strength progress support it.

sources.label: Butters University README — Training intensity, volume & frequency (bands, set counting, older adults)
Butters University README — Module: Energy balance (hold training volume during a cut)
Butters University README — Training case studies (Tom: 2 sessions/week, ~8–10 sets)

quotes: Anchor around 10–15 direct sets/week/muscle if intermediate, and move up cautiously
Push past ~20 direct sets only if recovery markers and continued strength progress support it
weighting indirect sets at roughly half
If you're training an older client (60+), the evidence points the other way
bu.note: BU sets both the band and the number. Intermediate starts at 12, low in BU's 10–15 anchor ('move up cautiously'; BU's worked example lands on ~11.5). Beginners start at 10 (BU: moderate volume beat high volume in untrained lifters). Advanced start at 15, leaving 15–20 for when progress and recovery support it. 60+ start at 10 (BU case study: 'closer to 10 sets/week/muscle'). Two sessions a week: 8–10 (BU case study Tom). A cut keeps volume (BU Energy balance: 'don't shortchange training volume during a cut'). Menno's formula is reported beside it as a comparison only (train.volume.henselmans).

statement: Comparison only — never sets the plan. Menno Henselmans volume formula: (f<3 ? f : 2.5) × 5 × recovery × energy-balance factor × √training status (+3 for women). The plan shows it next to the Butters University number (train.volume.bu) so the coach can compare.

quotes: Anchor around 10–15 direct sets/week/muscle if intermediate, and move up cautiously
bu.note: Differs from BU: the formula lowers volume in a deficit (BU says hold it), adds +3 sets for every woman (BU: only where in-session fatigue limits, not for every exercise), and runs above BU's bands (17.7 for an intermediate on 3 full-body days, 20.7 for a woman). That is why it is a comparison only.

statement: Training status for the volume formula from years of training: under 1 year = 1 (beginner), under 4 = 2, otherwise 3 (advanced). A starting point for the coach, not a cited figure.

bu.note: BU does not define training-status cut-offs by years of experience.

statement: Training split from weekly sessions: 1–3 full body, 4 upper/lower, 5 PPL + upper/lower, 6 PPL ×2.

quotes: frequency at least once/week per 6 sets of volume per muscle
Twice weekly per muscle is a safe, well-supported default
bu.note: Matches the 6-sets-per-session frequency rule and the twice-weekly default.

statement: At least one session per week for every 6 weekly sets of a muscle: flag more than 6 sets per muscle per session.

sources.label: Butters University README — Training intensity, volume & frequency; seed text from src/knowledge/training-methodology.js

quotes: frequency at least once/week per 6 sets of volume per muscle
bu.note: BU's frequency rule (once a week per 6 sets) read as a per-session limit of 6 sets. BU's worked example puts 7 direct-equivalent sets in one session and calls that comfortable, so the flag is advice, not a hard stop.

statement: Double progression in 6–12 reps: leave 1–3 reps in reserve on most sets, failure only on the last set of an exercise; add reps, then the smallest load increment.

sources.label: Butters University README — Exercise execution / technique; seed text from src/knowledge/training-methodology.js

quotes: Leave 1–3 reps in reserve on most sets; save all-out failure for the last set of an exercise, if at all
bu.note: RIR as BU says. 6–12 reps is roughly 70–85% 1RM, inside the 30–90% band BU's training-volume module gives; BU leaves the exact load to feel, so the range is a coaching default the coach can change.

statement: Deloads are reactive and per exercise: deload an exercise only when its performance unexpectedly drops (>2.5% strength loss at the same exercise with no other explanation). Scheduled every-4th-week deloads are not recommended.

sources.label: Butters University README — Periodization; seed text from src/knowledge/training-methodology.js

quotes: Trigger a deload based on evidence of accumulated fatigue (stalled lifts, rising soreness, poor sleep/recovery), not a fixed calendar date
bu.note: Matches: deloads react to fatigue and are not put on a calendar.

statement: Before the first exercise for a muscle group, do 1-3 progressively heavier submaximal sets of that exercise, ramping to the first working set: barbell lifts bar, ~50%, ~70% (+~85% when the work is 5 reps or fewer); other compounds ~50%, ~70% (+~85% likewise); isolation one set at ~50%. No static stretching or activation drills.

quotes: followed by 1-3 progressively heavier submaximal sets per exercise before working sets
use progressively heavier submaximal sets of the actual exercise instead
3 progressively-loaded squat sets (bar only, ~50%, ~70%, ~85%) before the working weight
Skip static stretching before training entirely
bu.note: Same ramp as BU's worked example (bar, ~50%, ~70%, ~85%). The app keeps the ~85% set for work of 5 reps or fewer, within BU's 1-3 sets, and picks rep counts (8/5/3/1) that BU does not give. 'First exercise per muscle group' comes from BU's case-study module, not the Warm-up section.
